walkthrough:
The Big Idea - Making Millions of Copies**
PCR is an in vitro method to amplify DNA. That means starting from just one tiny sample, you make millions of identical copies very rapidly. This is essential before sequencing, fingerprinting or cloning when starting material is too small.

Stage 1 - Denaturation at High Heat**
Heat the DNA to $95^\circ\text{C}$. This breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases and separates / denatures the double helix into two single template strands. No enzyme is needed for this separation, just heat.

Stage 2 - Annealing of Primers on Cooling**
Cool to $60-65^\circ\text{C}$ and add short single-stranded primer DNA. Primers attach to the ends of the target sequence by complementary base pairing - A with T, C with G. They provide a free 3-prime end for polymerase to start from and ensure only the wanted region is copied.

Stage 3 - Extension by Taq Polymerase**
Warm to $70-75^\circ\text{C}$, the optimum for Taq DNA polymerase. Taq adds free nucleotides complementary to the template, synthesising a new strand. Taq comes from a thermophilic bacterium so it is heat stable and is not denatured at $95^\circ\text{C}$, so it does not need replacing each cycle.

Cycling Gives Exponential Amplification**
The cycle of heat, cool, warm is repeated 20-30 times automatically. Each new strand becomes a template in the next cycle, so DNA doubles each time. That is why PCR is rapid, needs only a tiny starting sample, and is highly efficient.

Final answer: PCR produces large numbers of copies / amplifies a length of DNA rapidly from only a small sample. DNA is denatured / separated into two strands by heat at $95^\circ\text{C}$. Primer DNA is added, anneals at $60-65^\circ\text{C}$ by complementary base pairing. DNA / Taq polymerase replicates the template strand at $70-75^\circ\text{C}$. Mixture is heated again to separate strands and process is repeated. Taq polymerase is heat stable with high optimum temperature so is not denatured and does not need replacing each cycle, making process efficient.

walkthrough:
What a Plasmid Is**
A plasmid is a small, circular piece of double-stranded DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome. Its small size makes it easy to extract, manipulate in a test tube, and reintroduce into cells.

Independent and High Copy Replication**
Plasmids replicate independently of the chromosome, often with multiple origins of replication. This gives a high copy number, so one transformed bacterium makes many copies of the inserted gene automatically as the bacteria divide.

Easy to Engineer as a Vector**
Plasmids can be cut open with a restriction enzyme / endonuclease to give sticky ends, and the desired gene / DNA fragment can be inserted and ligated. The recombinant plasmid then acts as a vector to carry the foreign DNA into a bacterial host cell, which takes it up by transformation. Many also carry a promoter to drive expression of the gene.

Markers Allow Selection**
Plasmids often contain marker genes such as genes for antibiotic resistance. Only transformed bacteria survive on antibiotic plates, so this helps in identifying which bacteria have successfully taken up the plasmid.

Final answer: Plasmids are small circular double-stranded DNA that replicate independently with multiple origins, giving high copy number. Easy to extract from bacteria, can be cut with restriction enzyme / endonuclease so gene / DNA can be inserted. Can be taken up by bacteria so acts as a vector and may carry promoter for expression. May contain antibiotic resistance / marker genes to help identify transformed bacteria.
